Those are exactly the right questions to ask before starting — here's how I'd approach it:

## How often to strength train

**For a beginner runner: 2–3 sessions per week, full-body, on non-consecutive days.**

- **2x/week is a great starting point** for you. It's enough to build real strength, and it respects your running volume. (You've mentioned before that you prefer short 15–20 minute strength sessions tacked onto your morning workouts — that format fits perfectly here.)
- **Don't stack lower-body lifting on hard days.** Put strength on easy-run days or rest days, and try to keep heavy leg work at least a day away from your long run or a speed session.
- **Start with 2 sets of 8–12 reps**, 1–2 exercises per muscle group. Add a set or a little weight only when your last two reps still feel controlled with good form — the same gradual-progression rule as mileage.
- **Every 4–6 weeks, take a lighter week** (fewer sets or less weight) so your body can absorb the work.

**Signs you're overdoing it:** soreness lasting more than ~72 hours, joint (not muscle) pain, sleep or running performance dropping, or a noticeably elevated resting heart rate. Any of those mean back off for a few days.

## Warm-up for strength training

Your running warm-up is a good base, but strength work needs a bit more joint prep and muscle activation:

1. **5 minutes of general easy movement** — brisk walk, easy jog, bike, or jump rope to raise your temperature.
2. **Dynamic mobility:** leg swings (front/back and side to side), walking lunges with a reach, bodyweight squats, arm circles, cat-cow.
3. **Activation drills:** glute bridges, banded lateral walks, and a 20–30 second plank — this "wakes up" the glutes and core you're about to use.

Skip long static stretching *before* lifting on cold muscles — save it for after.

## Cool-down

This is where you can absolutely reuse your running routine:

- **5 minutes of easy movement** to bring your heart rate down.
- **Static stretches, 20–30 seconds each:** quads, hamstrings, hip flexors, glutes/piriformis, calves, plus a chest stretch if you did upper body.
- The stretches you already do after runs work fine here — if you run and lift on the same day, one combined cool-down covers both.

The short version: **2–3 short full-body sessions a week, spaced out, dynamic warm-up before, static stretching after.** That's a sustainable starting dose that won't derail your running.
